$$
(2+7\,\text{i})^{2}=(2+7\,\text{i})(2+7\,\text{i})

$$
\begin{aligned}(2+7\,\text{i})^{2} & =(2+7\,\text{i})(2+7\,\text{i}) \\  & =2\cdot 2+2\cdot 7\,\text{i}+7\,\text{i}\cdot 2+7\,\text{i}\cdot 7\,\text{i} \\  & =4+14\,\text{i}+14\,\text{i}+49\,{\text{i}}^{2} \\  & =4+28\,\text{i}+49\cdot (-1) \\  & =4+28\,\text{i}-49 \\  & =-45+28\,\text{i}.\end{aligned}

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Multiplying a purely imaginary number by a real number is similar to multiplying two monomials.

For example, we can multiply the purely imaginary number $3 \textrm{i}$ by the real number $6$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}6\cdot 3\text{i} & =(6\cdot 3)\text{i}=18\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we can multiply a complex number by a real number using the distributive property.

For example, we can multiply the complex number $2-3\textrm{i}$ by the real number $3$ as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
3(2-3\textrm{i}) &= 3\cdot2 + 3\cdot(-3\textrm{i}) \[3pt]
		&= 6 + 3\cdot (-3)\textrm{i} \[3pt]
		&= 6 -9\textrm{i}
	}
$$

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
Multiplying a purely imaginary number by a real number is similar to multiplying two monomials.

For example, we can multiply the purely imaginary number $3 \textrm{i}$ by the real number $6$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}6\cdot 3\text{i} & =(6\cdot 3)\text{i}=18\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we can multiply a complex number by a real number using the distributive property.

For example, we can multiply the complex number $2-3\textrm{i}$ by the real number $3$ as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
3(2-3\textrm{i}) &= 3\cdot2 + 3\cdot(-3\textrm{i}) \[3pt]
		&= 6 + 3\cdot (-3)\textrm{i} \[3pt]
		&= 6 -9\textrm{i}
	}
$$

tutorials.name: Multiplying by a Purely Imaginary Number
tutorials.problem:
Multiplying two purely imaginary numbers is similar to multiplying two monomials. But we also need to use the fact that $\textrm{i}^2=-1.$

For example, to multiply $2\textrm{i}$ and $3\textrm{i},$ we proceed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}(2\text{i})(3\text{i}) & =2\cdot 3\cdot {\text{i}}^{2} \\  & =6{\text{i}}^{2} \\  & =6(-1) \\  & =-6\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Knowing this, we can also multiply a complex number by a purely imaginary number.
For instance, to multiply $2\textrm{i}$ and $4-3\textrm{i},$ we use the distributive property and the fact that $\textrm{i}^2=-1\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		2\textrm{i}(4-3\textrm{i})
			&= 2\textrm{i}\cdot 4+2\textrm{i}\cdot(-3\textrm{i}) \[3pt]
&=2\cdot 4\textrm{i}+2\cdot(-3)\textrm{i}^2\[3pt]
&= 8\textrm{i}+(-6)(-1)\[3pt]
&= 8\textrm{i}+6\[3pt]

&=6+8\textrm{i}
	}
$$

tutorials.content:
Multiplying two purely imaginary numbers is similar to multiplying two monomials. But we also need to use the fact that $\textrm{i}^2=-1.$

For example, to multiply $2\textrm{i}$ and $3\textrm{i},$ we proceed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}(2\text{i})(3\text{i}) & =2\cdot 3\cdot {\text{i}}^{2} \\  & =6{\text{i}}^{2} \\  & =6(-1) \\  & =-6\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Knowing this, we can also multiply a complex number by a purely imaginary number.
For instance, to multiply $2\textrm{i}$ and $4-3\textrm{i},$ we use the distributive property and the fact that $\textrm{i}^2=-1\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		2\textrm{i}(4-3\textrm{i})
			&= 2\textrm{i}\cdot 4+2\textrm{i}\cdot(-3\textrm{i}) \[3pt]
&=2\cdot 4\textrm{i}+2\cdot(-3)\textrm{i}^2\[3pt]
&= 8\textrm{i}+(-6)(-1)\[3pt]
&= 8\textrm{i}+6\[3pt]

&=6+8\textrm{i}
	}
$$

tutorials.name: Multiplying Two Complex Numbers
tutorials.problem:
Finally, we can multiply two complex numbers just like multiplying two binomials. Again, we use the fact that $\mathrm{i}^2=-1.$

So, to multiply $2 + \textrm{i}$ and $5 + 3\textrm{i},$ we proceed as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
		(2+\textrm{i})(5+3\textrm{i}) &= 2 (5+3\textrm{i})  + \textrm{i} (5+3\textrm{i}) \
		 &= 2\cdot5 + 2\cdot(3\textrm{i}) +\textrm{i}\cdot 5+ \textrm{i} \cdot (3\textrm{i}) \
		&= 10 + 6\textrm{i} + 5\textrm{i} +3\textrm{i}^2 \
		&= 10 + 11\textrm{i} + 3(-1) \
		&= 10 + 11\textrm{i}  - 3 \
		&= 7 + 11\textrm{i}
	}
$$
tutorials.title: Multiplying Two Complex Numbers
tutorials.content:
Finally, we can multiply two complex numbers just like multiplying two binomials. Again, we use the fact that $\mathrm{i}^2=-1.$

So, to multiply $2 + \textrm{i}$ and $5 + 3\textrm{i},$ we proceed as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
		(2+\textrm{i})(5+3\textrm{i}) &= 2 (5+3\textrm{i})  + \textrm{i} (5+3\textrm{i}) \
		 &= 2\cdot5 + 2\cdot(3\textrm{i}) +\textrm{i}\cdot 5+ \textrm{i} \cdot (3\textrm{i}) \
		&= 10 + 6\textrm{i} + 5\textrm{i} +3\textrm{i}^2 \
		&= 10 + 11\textrm{i} + 3(-1) \
		&= 10 + 11\textrm{i}  - 3 \
		&= 7 + 11\textrm{i}
	}
$$
